utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-03-69-PT, The Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. May I have the appearances. Prosecution first.

utterances.speaker: MS. BREHMEIR-METZ
utterances.text: For the Prosecution, trial attorney Doris Brehmeir-Metz. The senior trial attorney on the case, Dermot Groome, offers his apologies to the Court for not being here today. He has to be in a session in Courtroom II, where is he on trial in the Lukic and Lukic case and has asked me to act on his behalf. With me, our Legal Officer Klaus Hoffman; Case Manager Thomas Laugel; and, in the back, Legal Intern Birte Brodkorb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Brehmeir-Metz. Mr. Groome is excused. Could I have the appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm Geert-Jan Knoops, lead counsel for Mr. Stanisic; escorted by Co-Counsel, Mr. Wayne Jordash; and our two legal assistants, Ms. Amy Walsh and Ms. Anne-Marie Verwiel. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And for Mr. Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I'm Attorney-at-Law Zoran Jovanovic, and Ms. Ingrid Morgan, Legal Assistant, is appearing with me today on behalf of our client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jovanovic. You may see that the Status Conference that the whole Bench is there, and I feel more comfortable to be assisted by those colleagues who are already familiar with the case. And apart from that, I think it is good to work together as much as possible. The last Status Conference was on the 12th of November, and I would first like to establish that the -- both accused are on provisional release and have given their written consent to proceed in their absence. I put this on the record. And since it's not in any way challenged, I'd like to continue that the last Status Conference was held on 12th of November, and since Status Conferences have to be held every 120 days we have scheduled a Status Conference for today. I'm, for the first time, with you in this case in its new -- in the new Chamber's composition. Counsel have received kind of a short agenda. Is that correct, Mr. Jovanovic, Mr. Knoops? We'll then follow that agenda. But I would like to start with the following. The -- I have been informed, of course, about the -- through the filings that have been made recently have been made, and we'll pay further attention to that soon, we have been informed about the development in the medical situation of Mr. Stanisic. Is there anything you would like to add to what has been already filed so that we have the full factual basis for any further discussion we may have this afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honour, although not being a medical expert, of course, our experience until so far with the accused has been consistent with the medical filings as of the provisional release.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I was not seeking that kind of information, Mr. Knoops. What I was seeking is whether anything came in, new reports, et cetera, what your evaluation of it is and whether you -- your observations are in line with -- is a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I just want to have the full factual basis that we didn't miss anything, if you, for example, would know as I know meanwhile that one of the reports we asked for will arrive a bit later, that's the kind of information I'm seeking. Mr. Jovanovic, anything you would like to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm addressing you, and I should have more properly formulated my question, because we are dealing with the filings in relation to Mr. Stanisic and what, of course, I wanted to ask you but did not clearly do, whether there's any information in relation to Mr. Simatovic, which -- of which the Chamber should be aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. Mr. Simatovic is fully abiding by the conditions of his provisional release, and the Court is informed about it regularly by the competent organs of the Republic of Serbia. His health condition is good and he is working on his case together with his Defence counsel. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. We'll then move on on the now established factual basis, and I would like to start with the decision by this Chamber then still in a different composition 17th of December 2008. In that decision, the adjournment of proceeding was prolonged beyond the original adjournment which was ordered on the 20th of May, 2008. The registry was then instructed to contact the two independent court experts, Dr. de Man, who is a psychiatrist, and Dr. Siersema, who is a gastroenterologist, to facilitate obtaining further reports, to be provided no later than three months from the date of this decision. These reports - and they have not been filed yet - are due no later than Tuesday, the 17th of March, and the Chamber will review upon receipt of these reports, the health condition of the accused Stanisic, for any appropriate further order. I already can inform you that Dr. Siersema, as I said before, has asked for a short delay, and he intends to file his report on the 23rd of March which is one week late. Since we have this report not available for us today, I don't think that it should cause a major obstacle to have this filed one week later. Is there any of the parties that would like to make any comment on this?

utterances.speaker: MS. BREHMEIR-METZ
utterances.text: No comments, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Further, in this decision of the 17th of December, the Chamber has ordered that Dr. Tarabar and Dr. Bucan, who are the treating gastroenterologists and the neuropsychiatrist, would continue to report to the Chamber at the end -- on a monthly basis at the end of each calendar month, and the reports to be received by the 9th of the next month, of the following month. Further, Dr. Tarabar was required to notify the Chamber of any hospitalisation for treatment, and the date of discharge, if he would have been discharged from hospital, and that information should be sent without delay. The Chamber observes at this moment that it seems that -- that there is no future compliance with respect to this order. Dr. Tarabar was late with his report, and since these reports have to be translated as well, that is of some concern to the Chamber. Further, we have not received any report from Dr. Bucan, although reference is made sometimes in Dr. Tarabar's reports about the area of expertise and area of treatment of Dr. Bucan. Of course, the Chamber expected to receive reports from both, but we will further -- we'll further see whether we have to give more clear instructions on that. So, therefore, any further orders or measures will be considered by the Chamber. Is there anything the party would say like to submit in relation to the reporting schedule and the reporting as it has taken place until now? Ms. Brehmeir.

utterances.speaker: MS. BREHMEIR-METZ
utterances.text: I apologise. All I wanted to comment in this respect is that the motion the Prosecution has announced as being planned to be filed would deal with these matters as well. That had been our intention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And asked already for permission to exceed the length of your submission. I'll first ask the Defence whether they have any submissions and are ready to, perhaps, briefly respond to the extent possible to the application for exceeding the length of the motion. Mr. Knoops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Of course, it's, I believe, not a matter for the Defence to interfere with the reporting system of the Military Academy. But it's just an observation from the bar table that the disposition of the Chamber of the 17th of December, paragraph 38, section D, orders Dr. Tarabar or in his absence Dr. Pecelj-Brocic and Dr. Bucan to continue to report. It doesn't say as such that they should separately report to the Chamber, and I noticed in the last report Dr. Tarabar filed of the 13th February of this year, reference is made to Dr. Bucan and his dealings with the patient. Although, I may admit that the report has not been signed by Dr. Bucan. So, I'm not sure, but that could have caused some kind of an unclarity for the two respective experts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But it seems to me -- let's not make a drama out of it, but that word "and" is sufficiently clear in the disposition under number -- paragraph 38, under D, and, of course, it's like asking a lawyer on tax matters to report on criminal matters. I think we have two experts. They have reported. They're invited to report, so I would very much encourage and we'll see how to achieve that. That we get the reports from those who have seen the patient, have examined the patient in this respect, and have -- have the sufficient expertise to report on that. Thank you for this. And what about the -- the request by Ms. Brehmeir-Metz for exceeding the length of the usual 3.000 words.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Clearly the issues are complex. On the other hand, we have had lengthy submissions and lengthy written motions on the subject. The issues have become quite clear. We're waiting on the latest reports, and we would submit brevity perhaps is something which would assist at this stage, given the length of the present proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Jordash, I think we still have to get used to each other. There is no clear "I object" or "I do not object." You are urging the Prosecution to be as brief as possible, in view of what we still expect. So therefore you do not oppose clearly and say, No, Ms. Brehmeir, you should stay within your 3 .000 words.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We don't oppose but we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. [Overlapping speakers] ... You do not oppose, but you urge for brevity rather than spending unnecessary words.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, we do seem to be going, to a degree, around in circles. The issues have become narrower, and we would submit they can be dealt with narrowly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Brehmeir-Metz, no objection. Mr. Jovanovic, I take it that you -- your client is not affected by the motion we expect from Ms. Brehmeir-Metz. Nevertheless, if would you like to say something about it, you're free to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. We have no comment as far as the part of the submission which we referred to the health condition of the Jovica Stanisic is concerned, but from this announcement of the OTP regarding this future filing, the question arises how far it will also refer to the accused Franko Simatovic and the possibility of continuing the trial, because I think that it is a bit unusual to ask in advance for exceeding the number of words without knowing in advance how much of it will be devoted to the health condition of the accused Jovica Stanisic, and how much to the possibility of the continuous of this trial, including that of the accused Mr. Simatovic. The OTP could file two motions. First of all, presenting it's position on the accused Jovica Stanisic, and finally, when we have a clear position about the OTP and the Trial Chamber on that particular issue, possibly only after that we could discuss the possibilities of the further continuation of the trial. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it the Office of the Prosecution has chosen to file a submission in which the two matters are dealt with. That is, what is the present medical situation; what does this mean in legal terms; and how are we going to proceed. Is that, in short, what you want to file?

utterances.speaker: MS. BREHMEIR-METZ
utterances.text: That is, in short, the gist of the motion and it is going affect the accused Franko Simatovic in the general terms that whatever affects the health status of Mr. Stanisic and the consequences to be drawn from that, for the further progress of the trial is, of course, also going to affect Mr. Simatovic. But it is it in -- in its gist it is going deal with Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, there's some uncertainty at this moment about the medical reports. May I take it, Ms. Brehmeir, that you'll wait until we have received the medical reports because otherwise we need a second filing, I take it, to update the Chamber, or do you -- are you not going to wait? Where you're expected to have to wait until the 17th, now you'll even have to wait until the 23rd.

utterances.speaker: MS. BREHMEIR-METZ
utterances.text: Our initial plan, Your Honours, had been to file this motion regardless of the income of the court-appointed experts prior to the 17th because there is a lot of subject matters that need to be dealt that are not touched upon or are not going to be touched upon by the court-appointed experts. We were considering the possibility of then filing a brief addendum dealing with the court-appointed experts' reports only, but I am, of course, happy to hear Your Honours' guidance on that and follow Your Honours' guidance. It is not a problem for the Prosecution to wait with the filing until the court-appointed experts have actually come in and can be covered by that motion as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any further submissions in relation to what Ms. Brehmeir told us? Mr. Knoops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have observed that the announcement of the Prosecution for permission to exceed word limit was also based on the premise that we are facing a new chamber, and the Prosecution, in its motion for permission to exceed the word limit, also refers to the fact that it would helpful to the new chamber to get a medical update of the existing medical evidence. So it's our submission that if it's the intention of the Prosecution to actually summarise what has been dealt with in the past, in terms of fitness or unfitness, such a motion seems to us quite superfluous with all due respect, and we would encourage also in view of the judicial economy that the Prosecution would file the motion after the court-appointed experts have submitted their reports. It seems to us more practical because in no way you can, I think, ignore the reports which are due to be filed in March. There will be submissions on the basis of these reports in any event I believe. So, in our view it would be simply more practicable that if the Chamber agrees and also the Prosecution to await those reports. And, again, I believe that filing a motion to update a new chamber is not exactly the way to file a motion. The Chamber has access to all medical materials from the past so that we don't believe this is a reason to file a separate motion from the perspective of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, anything to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. In the light of the position of the OTP, to the effect that every future decision regarding the accused Jovica Stanisic certainly produce an effect and have consequences also on the accused Simatovic. It is -- leads me to the position that it is not actually expedient to this because the health condition of the accused Stanisic before the court-appointed experts' reports arrive. This will certainly be a fact that the Trial Chamber will have to consider in handing down its ruling. I believe that that will be the expedient way to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jovanovic. Ms. Brehmeir-Metz, it even had not come to my mind that you want to be repetitious in that motion and to summarise; all the material is available to the Chamber, all the discussions about this are available to the Chamber as well. So the Chamber would certainly not appreciate, but, again, it had not yet come to my mind that you would intend to do that. The Chamber would certainly not appreciate if we start summarising the past. That's one. The Chamber, you asked for guidance. The Chamber would like you to you file such a motion after we've received the reports from the court-appointed experts, and the Chamber does not urge you, as suggested by Mr. Jovanovic, to split up the medical part and the procedural consequences. If you'd like to deal with them as, more or less, as a summarised before, that is okay as far as the Chamber is concerned. Anything else to be said about this subject? Then I'd like to move to the next topic, which is pending motions. There are several decisions pending on motions which concern subject matters that are best left to the Chamber, which will conduct the trial. It was at the 12th of November of last year's Status Conference that Judge Robinson identified these as being the motions brought under Rules 92 bis, 92 ter, and 92 quater as well as motions for protective measures, motions for testimony by way of video-conference link, or motions concerning submission of expert witness reports, and a motion for judicial notice of adjudicated facts. As far as adjudicated facts are concerned, there has since the last Status Conference, there has been a second Prosecution motion filed the 12th of December, 2008, and the Stanisic Defence filed a request for an extension of time; and the Simatovic Defence has filed its response to second Prosecution motion for judicial notice. I think the last one was about the -- the facts taken from -- the 213 facts taken from the Martic trial. The Chamber considers that it would be useful to make progress in this respect. The Chamber can't force you to agree on certain matters. However, adjudicated facts, of course, are to this extent, different, that it's not agreement an anything. It's just -- and that's what I expected the party would do, to comment on the admissibility of these facts as adjudicated facts. Now to some extent at least the Simatovic Defence has done so. At the same time, I must admit that I do not fully understand, for example, facts where apparently you that judicial notice will be taken by this Chamber of adjudicated facts, where I really have great difficulties to understand where the problem might lie. I just give one example. The -- for example the Cerovljani, Dubica, and Bacin proposed facts number 190, reads: "Krcine is on the outskirts of Bacin and less than a ten-minute walk from the Catholic church in Bacin." Now this has been -- I should say that it's number 98 on the list and it's dealt with in paragraph 190 in the Martic judgement. I have great difficulties to understand for what reason a party would oppose this adjudicated fact. Mr. Jovanovic could be help me out to understand what made you oppose against everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence has formulated its position in both of our responses to the Prosecution's motions. It is our general position that regardless of the fact, even though previously the Defence said that it will reconsider this issue, we see it as an ongoing matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... has the Chamber been informed about any reconsideration and in the -- one of the latest filings by the Prosecution, it was said that despite the offer to reconsider, nothing has happened in the field of adjudicated facts and I, on the 17th of November, it was clear that everyone said we will reconsider. If you reconsider something that either results in something, in which case, of course, Ms. Brehmeir-Metz would like to know and she says nothing. Or would you inform the Chamber or you would tell that reconsideration has not brought anything. And, therefore, I'm just asking you now, I take one example - I could take many others - what -- is Krcine not on the outskirts of Bacin, is it more than a ten-minute walk from the Catholic church, or is there no Catholic church in Bacin? What's the use of not making progress in this respect? Again, if there is a serious challenge to this fact, apart from how important that will be in this case, then please tell me what caused you to, among other things, oppose this as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you want me to be quite specific about this very fact that you quoted, this is part of the position as presented by the Defence, simply speaking these are facts that have been taken out of context, in our view. Each such fact was contained in a more general description in one of the locations from the crime base. It is the position of Defence that by accepting these fact, we will put ourselves in the position where we will be prejudiced. Our situation will be more difficult during the trial when it comes to establishing the facts about, say, the village of Bacin. And by doing so, by accepting this fact, we would give advantage to the Prosecution, which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... accepting this fact I think. What you are -- what you are requested to do is to tell us whether this fact, which was adjudicated, whether it would be permissible to take judicial notice of it. There is - as the case law is clear - that if you want to challenge these facts, please do so. No problem. You can do it. But, of course, then have you to come up with something serious. That is if on an evaluation of evidence which was not further challenged and which is final, if a Trial Chamber has established a certain fact, then that fact, again, can be taken judicial notice of if all the requirements of the case law and the rule on adjudicated facts are met. Now, what you say it was bring us in a bad position. It's crime base and we would admit that these facts have occurred. What actually happens is the following: That you give a sweeping statement or crime base taken out of context, et cetera, not acceptable, which gives the Chamber no guidance. If you would say, Look at those five, look at what they say there, we are not -- we are opposing against taking judicial notice of this, because we have good reasons A, B, C, and D to say that these five are not correct. That it was a misappreciation, that the evidence which we are able to bring before this chamber will certainly undermine the evidence that was before the other chamber. We will make a serious effort. Then we know what we are talking about, but to say, 231, all crime base. No. It's -- that is not the best way of drawing the attention of this Chamber to the real issues. And if you say, All the crime base is the issue, it's all taken out of context, then, of course, we'd like to know what the proper context is. You're not saying the facts are wrong, apparently. You're saying it's taken out of context. Then please present the right context to us and give an indication as what that context, the proper context would be. We are talking about small facts, and the Chamber would like to know to what extent there are serious objections against taking judicial notice of them. That's the issue, in my view, and, therefore, just a -- everything out position, I think at an earlier stage there were 33 that were not opposed. I think the case law of this Tribunal gives clear guidance on what kind of objection against proposed adjudicated facts is taken seriously, and if you just say, We oppose everything, that certainly will not focus the attention of the Chamber on what the real issues will be. Mr. Jovanovic, that's my brief comment at this moment and, of course, it's meant to be an encouragement to -- to further look at it. Do you have anything you'd like to bring to my attention in respect of these matters or if there's any question, if you would like to seek any further guidance, then ... so it's clear what the Chamber would expect more or less, what would -- what kind of debate we would have between the parties on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No thank you, Your Honours. I don't need further guidance. As I have said earlier, in our direct contact with the Prosecution, we have announced the possibility of reconsideration of adjudicated facts after the Martic judgement. We made no promises to the Prosecution that we would accept in, and later on we presented our position formally in writing. Nevertheless, we will accept your suggestion, and despite the fact that the Prosecution submitted a motion for facts to be accepted and even though we gave two responses to the OTP motion, we still believe that it is possible for us to have direct contacts with the Prosecution and to further clarify this matter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I encourage you to have further contacts with the Prosecution on the matter. I'm paying so much attention to this because this is one of the few areas where we could make progress. There are a few others which are suffering a bit from -- from a kind of paralysis. Mr. Knoops, what I just said to Mr. Jovanovic, of course, would be for the further conversations. Any further positions to be taken would be relevant for the Stanisic Defence as well because on the 17th of November I think you also said that you would further -- you would perhaps reconsider some of the submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, we find ourselves in difficulty in this way. That, as Your Honours and as you -- you know, our client is suffering from severe illnesses. We have a client who once upon a time was able to give us clear and forceful instructions. And we have a client who we know, if he was in a fit state, would wish to do so on this matter. We also have a client who, if and when he becomes well again, we know will be unhappy if he has not had the opportunity to contribute to this important discussion, especially as it relates to important issues such as the -- if I may call it the Martic crime base. So we are in that difficulty in terms of practical consideration to our client. We also consider ourselves in some difficulty ethically in that we are assigned to him, and we would wish to act on his instructions, especially when it comes to evidential matters, and we regard that assignment in the sense that first and foremost we look to him for our instructions. We, of course, secondarily or perhaps equally look to assist the Court. But our first focus as assigned is to look to Mr. Stanisic. In addition to that, the second complication is that we do keep getting from the Prosecution motions adding significant pieces of evidence. So it's not that we can look back at the instructions we once had from Mr. Stanisic and say, Well, we got sufficient to go with those instructions, because we cannot have that confidence when we are being served with, well, certainly the Prosecution are attempting to add -- well, on the 20th of January 83 documents. A considerable significance. So we -- these are our difficulties, and whilst we, of course, want to assist the expeditious and fair progress of the trial, we would ask for a degree of sympathy when it comes to issues which, whilst not binding us, we know our client will be unhappy with any, if you like, concession even those which are not bound -- we are not bound by ultimately. He is, in our respectful submission, the real expert in our case, and we cannot rely upon him at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps adjudicated facts is one of the best examples to demonstrate that the case law on it is of a very technical nature. Well, I do not whether you are waiting for Mr. Stanisic's comments in the legal/technical sense. I would say on many other subjects and apart from sympathy, all Defence counsel have our sympathy. That is -- but, of course, you asked for it in a specific context, Mr. Jordash. This is, I would say, prima facie, the area where the evaluation of the evidence. You have access to the files, to the context of the judgement, you can check whether the matter has been raised on appeal, yes or no. You can check all these kind of things where, if you do not get detailed instructions in that respect, I would say that would be far more vital in many other respects where I have -- which I have not addressed at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] We can look and look at the threshold legal tests, but in terms of whether the facts are something which we will seek to oppose or seek to, if you like, re-establish during our case, we are to a degree dependent on the case we're going to run.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But that has got nothing to do with taking judicial notice of the agreed facts -- of facts which were established by another Trial Chamber. Because still if you think - and I think I explained to Mr. Jovanovic before - if you think that establishing these facts was a clear mistake, they didn't have the evidence, they evaluated the evidence in a wrong way, of course, it takes a bit more to challenge adjudicated facts than just facts that you consider not to be proven or not to be fully proven by the Prosecution because it has been already subject of extensive litigation often or -- and a lot of facts are excluded if they are just agreed upon and not established by the Chamber on the base of the evidence. There aren't any -- I mean, the case law is quite clear on that. And, therefore, if at a certain moment you would say -- well, first of all, there may be many, I just gave one. I don't know whether you've consider it's more than a ten-minutes walk from Bacin, but I would be surprised if that would be become the issue in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It's as I sought to argue, it is the issue, one that the accused has information which would assist us with making these decisions, but it is also the additional ethical element of not wanting to consider these issues without our client, who provides us with instructions. I understand what Your Honour is saying in terms of the legal significance of adjudicated facts, but nevertheless this is something we would have ordinarily have wished to sit down with our client and discuss, and he would have taken a full role in it as he did until his illness prevented him. And so we, of course, want to assist, but at the same time - and this is why I used the word "sympathy" - because this is an ethical consideration as well, which isn't something which necessarily lends itself to tangible explanation. We feel ethically obliged to have him well before making decisions which he would wish to participate in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, there are two elements in this. The first is that you - and I fully understand that - want to give proper and full attention to what your client tell you -- tells you. At the same time, at this moment, the procedural situation is that no unfitness to stand trial or unfitness to give instruction has been established. That may be different once we have received the other reports. But, of course, on the basis of the decisions taken by the Chamber until now, there's no good reason to accept that the illness prevents him from giving instructions. I do understand that you have not received instructions, that you have your own opinion about the reasons for that. I certainly take it that we'll pay further attention it to once we have received the other reports. But that is the procedural situation we find ourselves in at this moment. Yes, Mr. Knoops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: May I just clarify one thing, Your Honour. I think there is -- otherwise, we are quite confusing also from our perspective. The basis of our motion is not that we as Defence will oppose any of the adjudicated facts. The basis of our motion is that in light of the fact that in November, indeed during the Status Conference, I informed the legal officer that we would be willing to reconsider our position, that after the Status Conference, the motion was filed on the 12th of December, containing 26 pages annexed with 230 proposed adjudicated facts amounting to 11 pages of legal argumentation. That is the main foundation, Rule 127, in light of the handicap we are facing irrespective of fitness or not. So the basis of the foundation is not that we will oppose anything which is adjudicated or not. The basis is that we simply do not have sufficient time and sources to responsibly respond to an adjudicated facts motion containing 230 proposed adjudicated facts. That is the main foundation of the motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the earlier motions, how many did you oppose to and how many did you not oppose to? I mean, we're now talking about a 213 recently filed but we have, of course, all the series with quite a number. What's exactly there the progress made?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we have first motion which we responded to. This is the second motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: On adjudicated facts so ... Prosecution received our responses to the first adjudicated facts motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And any further -- was that the one where 33 were out of 450 or how many there were --

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that you did not oppose. A minimal number? 33 is the number which is still on my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm informed that indeed that motion was partly opposed, since most of the alleged adjudicated facts went to the conduct of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will -- and we'll further have a look at that, and I certainly -- I do now understand that it's mainly -- that it was recently filed and its resources with the handicap and not with the real obstacle. Whether that will change in the future, we'll see that. Would it be a good idea if the parties would just make clear appointments. Say, in two weeks we'll go through the -- for example, through the easy ones. If I could just give you a suggestion, Mr. Knoops, for -- number 64, Martic trial judgement 173, Cerovljani is situated above 3 to 6 kilometres north of Hrvatska Dubica and in 1990 its population was some 500 people. What it takes is a map and a -- the margin is even 3 kilometres on that distance, and what we need is the, I would say the 1990 census to see whether it's approximately 500 people. Let's try to get -- let's try to make progress, rather than to discuss on why no progress can be made. I think I have said enough about the adjudicated facts. Now, you may have understood that the Chamber urges you that in one of the few fields where progress can be made that it will be made. Any further submissions in relation to this? Ms. Brehmeir-Metz.

utterances.speaker: MS. BREHMEIR-METZ
utterances.text: Just very briefly respond to what we've heard now. It is indeed precisely the kind of facts that Your Honour has just pointed at from the second adjudicated facts motion that the Prosecution proposed in its recent, most recent proposal, to find an agreement on facts. It was precisely that kind of facts mere crime base facts or the names and identities of victims that were killed in the incidents, at the crime bases, that the Prosecution has proposed to find agreement on, but regrettably those proposals were, first of all, not responded to at all. And what we now hear, and I have set that out in the recent motion requesting the hearing that we are at now, the argument of certainly Mr. Stanisic's Defence, we have just heard; namely, we don't receive proper instructions. And I can just reiterate what Your Honour has just said. We have a fitness motion that says the accused, regardless of his chronicle illness, is able to instruct counsel, and what is required here is not that the accused is able to provide to his counsel daily instruction in relation to all the details of the case. What the Prosecution submits is totally sufficient is that he gives certain basic guidance and leaves further decisions to discretion of counsel. That, we would submit, is what counsel is here for. And, therefore, I can only stand by Your Honour and reiterate that the Prosecution, of course, remains open for any discussion on agreed facts. However, I venture to say that I fear progress is going to be difficult to achieve.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Certainly for the record, we would wish to make clear that whilst we recognise the uncertainty of the position as concerns Mr. Stanisic's fitness vis-a-vis legal definition, we would wish the Court to know that it is our experience with him, which leads us to confirm that he is unable to provide instructions to us. Now, whether this is an medical reason for that we don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, may I take it that you wanted to say that he doesn't give instructions. You said he is unable experience -- in your experience that he's unable, which is an interpretation, already, of what you can observe; that is, that he doesn't, when invited to do so, that he doesn't give instructions, which is not the same as that he is unable to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You're right, Your Honour. But what we would say is this. We've tried and he has, in our view, tried but what we -- the place with arrive at is not terribly coherent, and my learned counsel at the beginning said, Our experience with him has been consistent with the medical evidence. And it's, again, I use the word "sympathy" because it's right. We have a position which is legally unclear, but we have to work with this position on a practical level. And, yes, there's an implication which comes from the Prosecution on a regular basis that he is -- he's making it up. And we cannot say with certainty he isn't, but what we can say is that when we've tried he appears to try and yet is not able to give us coherent instructions [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Jordash. Soon we'll know more, I take it. We will then have received the latest medical reports and whether the procedural status in any way then changes or not, we'll see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then let's move on. As far as the Chamber is -- yes, as far as the agreed facts are concerned, they were briefly raised. I raised the adjudicated facts. They're, of course, the same counts; that is, draw the attention of the Chamber to matters that are really in dispute and that matter in this case. The parties themselves are best able to see whether it's just difficult to accept the evidence which is there or to assess that there is important evidence which, undermines the Defence evidence which undermines the Prosecution evidence. And again, if you ask our attention for 100 items, whereas ten are vital, then most of the time on the remaining 90 items is wasted time, and you will be less successful in focussing our attention on what really is the core of the case. That is apart from adjudicated facts which is even a bit easier, I would say, than agreed facts, may guide you in your further conversations. Next issue is disclosure, unless anything would be anything to be added.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Also, I think it's important for the Bench to note that in order to take away any impression that Defence counsel is not trying to do their best in order reach an agreement on either adjudicated or agreed facts. As Your Honours may know, we have filed a response on the Prosecution request for an oral hearing on the 19th of February, 2009, with a confidential annex. That annex includes a statement of our Defence team, page 2 at the first paragraph. Of course, it's confidential; I will not repeat it in public. And if Your Honours will be so kind to take that paragraph before you, I ask your attention for the first two sentences of that letter we sent to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the 19th of February submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You referred to -- you asked our attention for?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: First paragraph, page 2 of the letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Which is confidential annex to our --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: -- response. Your Honours may observe that we have drafted a document in which we go into many of the agreed facts. Yet for the reasons it set out in that paragraph, we feel not at liberty to file that draft in this stage, in light of the medical evidence we are facing. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I must admit, Mr. Knoops, that I have your response here, but the confidential annex I haven't got at this moment. Mr. Pittman will provide me with -- I couldn't take the whole file with me, and I didn't know you would ... Yes, I have it in front of me. It's page 2, first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: So, to make a long story short, we have actually a response made available for the Prosecution which we think, as Defence counsel, we could submit -- but yet because of the situation as it is currently still there, we believe that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the current procedural situation --

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- is that there's -- that Mr. Stanisic could not attend trial hearings in this courtroom, and whether that is still the case is still to be considered. But from the possibility to instruct or anything like that is a procedural situation that he is considered to be able to do that. Let me just see whether ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As I said before, the situation, procedurally is at this moment, it has not been established that he is not in a position to give instructions. Further, of course, we could -- but perhaps not -- this would not be the right moment or not, the level of detail of instructions, of course, is considered in a common law tradition quite differently in many jurisdictions. Some would just want him, an accused, to choose who he wants to be represented by, how to plead, whether he wants to appear as a witness in his own case, et cetera. But that's very limited. So to the extent -- what actually are the merits of any reliance on the inability of Mr. Stanisic to give you instructions is to be considered soon. The procedural situation at present is that it has not been established that he cannot, and therefore, the Chamber, with the sympathy you asked for, is, of course, proceeding on this basis. We can't just on your subjective feelings where the Trial Chamber has decided otherwise not -- not just say, Okay, take as much time as you want. And I'm not in doubt of your good intentions in this respect and therefore it's good that you have drawn our attention to that Annex A, to your response, which is a confidential annex. Anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I just raise just for Your Honours' attention. I don't wish to repeat myself, but simply --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're invited not to do so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I will be very brief. It's simply that -- it' s not, with the greatest of respect, an issue of simply our subjective assessment. We -- the latest psychiatric report gave Mr. Stanisic a GAF score of 31 to 40 which indicates impaired judgement and that -- the practical situation we find ourselves in, that we approach our client who has this, according to the latest psychiatric evidence, [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... let's not put forward the one psychiatric report which favours, others may be there which do not favour. Therefore, as I said before, we'll receive soon further medical examination, further medical reports, and I did not intend to say that it's just your subjective views. Of course, they will be supported by something, but it's -- at this moment your interpretation on the basis of your selection of the material.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I won't belabour the point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next point, disclosure. As far as the Chamber is aware, there are no outstanding disclosure issues. Is that correct? If everyone is silent on disclosure issues, I take it that it is correct. Ms. Brehmeir, you do not feel guilty at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MS. BREHMEIR-METZ
utterances.text: I don't hear anything from the Defence, which in itself is a good sign. What I had intended to say was that Mr. Hoffman would address you on disclosure issues, because he's dealing with that in the Prosecution team. But, actually, there is not much we have to report on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There appears nothing to be important enough to bring to our attention. And, Mr. Hoffman, you do not feel guilty at this moment in any way of not having disclosed anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMAN
utterances.text: No Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's good.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just informed by my legal assistant, Ms. Amy Walsh, that there are some minor disclosure problems that we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Worthwhile mentioning that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: We can deal that with a letter to the Prosecution. We're not going bore the Chamber with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I hope you still do not feel guilty after you've received that letter, Mr. Hoffman. Mr. Jovanovic, anything you would like to raise in relation to disclosure?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you, Your Honours. The possibly minor problems that have cropped up will be able to be solved in direct contact with the OTP. For the time being, having reviewed the disclosed material, the Defence has not found some things which are on the list, possibly it is an omission on our part. If not, I shall get in touch with our colleagues from the OTP. I believe we will be able to settle that quickly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If anything remains after that, the Chamber, of course, is always willing to assist the parties in resolving it. Then I move to the next subject. Any other matters to be raised? Let's start with the Defence. Mr. Jovanovic, any other matter not yet dealt with that you'd like to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Knoops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. None.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Brehmeir-Metz.

utterances.speaker: MS. BREHMEIR-METZ
utterances.text: None from the Prosecution, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then this concludes this Status Conference. I'm afraid that we can't set a date yet for the next Status Conference. The Rules tell us that it should be within 120 days, but much depends, of course, on the Chamber's review of the reports which we'll receive soon, the report of the independent court expert in relation to the health condition of Mr. Stanisic. Once we have reviewed them, we will issue an appropriate order, and whether that would be a Scheduling Order or whether it would be an order to invite the party for further submissions is still to be seen. But we will then issue the appropriate order. We stand adjourned, sine die.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the Status Conference adjourned at
